lines.text: Boots are by the fire. They were wringing wet when you came in, so I moved them, and I'll not be thanked for it.

Bed's made up at the back and the kettle's on. Sleep the night through and your animals will be right by the morning. If one of them won't settle, you knock on my door and I'll come up. Now then. Is it just the room, or will you be wanting your supper as well?

The rooms sit out over the water on the stilts, so they move all night. Nothing to be done about that. The door at the foot of the stair swells in the wet, so put your shoulder to it. You'll lie down and you'll decide you're not going to sleep. The man in the end room last week told me so at some length, and I could hear him through the floor by ten.
You'll sleep. Same money either way, mind. Your creatures will be sound again by the time you come down.

We let by the day here. The night's when the market's open, so nobody in this town wants a bed at night. Four, five, six — that's the linen. Where was I. Day rate, and I'd sooner have the money now than chase you for it later.

Your animals come down fit for the evening. That's what most people take a day room for. Key's on the hook by the stair, take it up yourself. And if you want the room again tomorrow, tell me before you go out tonight, or it's let at dawn to whoever comes off the market.
Vent side's warmer and it shakes. Other side's quiet and it's cold. People ask me for the quiet side, and then at two in the morning they're down the stairs wanting the vent side.

Your creatures will pick up overnight. I've not had one yet that didn't. Tubs are filled straight off the hot spring, which costs me nothing, so you'll come out of it clean as well. How are you keeping? Good. Soap's on the ledge by the door.
Shutters stay open. Top and bottom, all night, every room. That's rule eleven, and the rules in this town are the observatory's, not mine.

The observatory made me read the whole list out loud when I took the place on — twenty-two rules, and I could not tell you what the other twenty-one are. So you'll sleep with the cold coming straight in off the vale, and your animals will have come round by daylight all the same. There's a third blanket in the press on the landing.
Snares and salve. Tonic's on the shelf behind me. A plain snare comes in under a salve.

Bait mats are in that crate by your knee — I've not sorted them, so dig. A cheap mat is made up for a whole sort of animal at once, so anything of that sort will come to it. The dear ones are cut for one animal and nothing else, and they cost three times as much.

What goes in a mat is whatever the animal you're after eats. If you don't know what it eats, I'm not the one to ask — warden's down at the field station. Four mats left in that crate and the carter's not up till the week's end.

Reed bait's the bundle on the end of the trestle. There's nothing out there but Reedrick will look at it, and Reedrick are only through here in the summer, so that bundle has sat where it is since the thaw. Every few days I turn it over so the underside doesn't go green on me.
Salve, though. Salve moves. Everybody comes off that marsh cut about the hands, and I sell more of it in a wet week than I sell reed bait in a year.

Tonic as well, when I've got it in, and I've none in this week. Prices move with the fishery levy — the fishery levy, mind, not the harbour toll, because people hear levy and think toll. The levy's set at the town office and not by me. Ask Odo. He's down at the boats most days and he'll take his time about it.
Night market. Dusk to dawn, and no, we don't do mornings. Why don't we do mornings? There's nobody out in the mornings. I'm certainly not.

Lamp oil, spare wicks, tonic, silk by the bolt — evening to you! — silk by the bolt. And come the autumn a Gloomoth will drop onto the rail beside you and everybody just steps round it. It's after the moss on the rail. It hasn't even noticed there's a stall here.

The heavy snares, the ones that'll hold near enough anything — you'll be wanting one of those, of course you will, and I haven't got one. They come up here twice a year and they're gone the same night. Twice a year. Well. Once. The once was two winters back, so I'm about due another one.
No heavy snares since the contract closed. No tonic this month either — the cart comes up when the cart comes up.

What I've got is plain snares, salve and the ash bait. The ash bait brings an Ashvole and it brings nothing else, so there's no cheap one to stand beside it. The cheap bait used to come up on the Company cart, and there's no Company cart now. My prices went up the month the store next door boarded its windows.

If one of yours comes to the end of its years and leaves a relic, Bram takes it at the forge, and he'll want an ingot to go with it. I don't keep ingots. Never have. Shaft-head store's up the hill behind me and they'll sell you an ingot.
You'll want the other tin. That one's for the wick; the fill's in the flat tin at the end of the shelf.

Wispurr bait only moves in the winter. Winter's when the Wispurr are about, and the week the frost sets I'll shift every tin on that shelf inside two evenings. So I buy it in the autumn and sit on it. If you want a tin in the summer I'll sell you one, and it'll have gone hard, and it'll cost you the same.

Lamp oil, tonic, and a heavy snare in the drawer that I've had eighteen months. Take the pint of oil over the half if you're walking up the vale tonight. The observatory takes its lamps off Ingram direct, wheeled past this door on a handcart every autumn, the whole lot of them. What they want with that many, I don't ask and they don't say.
